Nigel Mackay PHD

New South Wales, Australia

He is author of the monograph, Motivation and Explanation: An Essay on Freud's Philosophy of Psychology, and a number of articles on philosophical and methodological issues in psychology and psychoanalysis.

In a coherent psychoanalysis, clinical language must be compatible with psychoanalytic theory and metatheory—the model of mind. The concepts of desire and symbolization are fundamental to the psychoanalytic model of mind, and this requires that we understand that behaviors and acts are indeed enactments: symbolic acts carried out as the consequence and manifestation of desires in turn derived from basic drives. Yet this sets up some puzzles where concepts valuable for expressing analytic facts and insights are in some tension with the general model of mind. One is that of substitute satisfaction: How exactly are we to understand this? The second, related to the first, is that of phantasy which is widely taken to be the realm within which substitute satisfaction works to effect some pacification of the underlying desires: How may we retain this important notion without undermining the realism of the psychoanalytic metapsychology?

This is an informative and thought-provoking book. Subtitled “A post-Kleinian approach to the treatment of primitive mental states,” it offers an integrated presentation of the key concepts and theoretical formulations of Wilfred Bion, Frances Tustin, Donald Winnicott, Esther Bick, Donald Meltzer, and other post-Kleinian British psychoanalysts of the Independent School. These formulations—“the container and the contained” (Bion), the formation of a “second skin” and “adhesive identification” (Bick), “autistic encapsulation” and “autistic shapes” (Tustin), “fear of breakdown” and “primitive agony” (Winnicott)—have to do with the earliest stages of mental development and the dynamics of the mother-infant dyad. Much of this work, particularly that of Frances Tustin, with whom Dr. Mitrani has had extensive communication, derives from the study and treatment of autistic and psychotic children. Dr. Mitrani contributes new conceptualizations of her own, e.g., “adhesive pseudo-object relations” and “unmentalized experience,” in the process of demonstrating the application and utility of these ideas to the treatment of “ordinary” adults who reveal a hidden, shut-away part of themselves stemming from some very early embryonic, fetal, or infantile experience of unbearable suffering or traumatic separation. In defense against such suffering they have evolved “extra-ordinary protections”—somatic, autistic, and psychotic—for purposes of psychic survival:

In the face of unbearable happenings occurring before birth and beyond, certain experiences are never had by the infant, and mental and emotional growth is subsequently truncated. However, such happenings do remain alive-if-encapsulated. Maintained in a kind of stasis, these are often reactivated by ordinary and extra-ordinary life events and, in the course of the psychoanalytic process, the opportunity arises for them to actually be experienced in the transference. Subsequently, development may once more be set in train. (p. 157)

The author traces the vicissitudes of a thirty-year analysis. The patient came into analysis as a suicidally depressed teenager, and has become a confident, content wife and mother of four. Among the most intense conflicts that were worked through were transference issues related to abandonment. The patient was given up for adoption at birth, and during the course of the analysis, developed a longing to be reunited with her biological mother. The author understands this longing as a displacement and avoidance of the pain of the transferential fear of the analyst repeating her history of rejection and abandonment. Through fits and starts, through the patient repeatedly leaving the analysis, and the analyst searching her out to come back, this analysis is testament to the power of self-transformation that is possible when historical repetitions are resolved.

This is a study of psychic movement, fluctuation, and change over a four year period in the treatment of a 41-year-old man fixated at a pre-object level of emotional development and exhibiting a range of psychotic symptoms including fragmentation of thought, obliteration of feeling, distortion of speech, confusion and loss of the boundaries of the self, and the destruction of his apparatus of awareness in the processing of stimuli. Transformations of the patient's representation of himself and of the analyst observed over the course of the first three years of treatment led to the research question, “How does the patient create psychic structure out of chaotic disorganization?” The methodology devised to study this question describes three comprehensive and overlapping axes of observation, whereby the functioning of the patient's apparatus of awareness, the evolution of his representation of himself, and his progressive construction of the analyst can be simultaneously tracked in either a progressive or regressive direction. The principal finding is that the patient creates psychic structure in the evolution and progression of transference states which the unconsciously enacts in the treatment. The uses the patient makes of the analyst and of the analytic setting constitute creative achievements in building psychic structure. Further, each such transformation of the analyst constitutes a transformation of the self in a progressive direction, structure being added by phases upon those that preceded. A sequence of four distinct phases describes the transformative movement from a fundamentally

263

objectless state to symbiosis to the construction of an externally situated transference object built out of fragments of the emerging self.

In this unique book thirteen prominent psychotherapy clinician-researchers (all but one a psychologist and only one a psychoanalyst) reflect candidly and often humorously on the “dynamic tension” of engaging in these two very different pursuits, personally balancing two different orientations to accruing and applying knowledge and understanding what works in psychotherapy. The editors note the difficulty they had in finding willing contributors to the volume, clinical researchers who were comfortable writing about their personal balancing act in conducting their activities. The resulting volume is a valuable set of essays on the value and difficulty of conducting valid clinically relevant research, and the necessity of informing research with insights from practice and vice versa. It also is an excellent resource for clinical researchers interested in selecting measures for their own research, as the contributors reflect and evaluate what symptom scales, coding systems, and observational techniques have been useful in their work on understanding the process and outcome of psychotherapy. While the authors represent a range of theoretical and clinical orientations, many of the qualitative techniques and design issues are of interest to the psychoanalytic clinical researcher.

The question of the death instinct has been a controversial one since Freud first introduced the concept in 1920. Many analysts dispute the dual drive theory, finding the idea that there is an unconscious demand on the mind to destroy, undo connections and return the organism to an inanimate state to be depressing and unsavory. This paper presents a patient whose major focus in treatment was a fascination with death, and attempts to understand and explain some of the dynamics associated with this phenomenon.

Dany Nobus PHD

Dany Nobus

Dany Nobus   Senior Lecturer in Psychology and Psychoanalytic Studies at Brunel University, and Visiting Professor at the Boston Graduate School for Psychoanalysis. Author, most recently, of Jacques Lacan and the Freudian Practice of Psychoanalysis (Routledge 2000).

The decline of the paternal function has often been used by social scientists and health professionals as an explanation for the occurrence of crippling psychosocial symptoms such as juvenile delinquency, drug abuse, racism and vandalism. Emboldened by Jacques Lacan's emphasis on the Name-of-the-Father as the stabilizing principle of the symbolic order, psychoanalysts in Europe have recently resurrected this theme in order to take issue with explicit changes in public policy making and more insidious modifications in social living conditions. In arguing for the maintenance of the symbolic father function, against alternative kinship patterns, psychoanalysts have thereby echoed the voices of neo-conservative, right-wing ideologists in their campaign for the restoration of the nuclear family. Yet the history of fatherlessness within twentieth century discursive practices shows that there is no evidence whatsoever for the causal link between the paternal function and psychosocial stability. Drawing on Derrida's deconstruction of Fukuyama's social optimism in The End of History it is demonstrated that the spectre of fatherlessness, whether conjured up within social theory or within psychoanalysis, reflects a severe crisis in knowledge within existing ideologies of meaning and serves the purpose of securing an epistemological status quo.

The case of Anna O, along with being a clear demonstration of the talking cure, is an example of induced deception where the true meaning of actions or symptoms is disguised. Anna's theatrical symptoms have become the model for a “theatre of cure” created by Breuer and Freud. The contemporary psychoanalytic community continues to misrepresent the case to defend against various forms of awareness, the most serious being the role of destructive aggression in Anna's pathology and Breuer's destructive actions, which inflicted harm on his patient.

Biblical commentators have variously interpreted the meanings of biblical texts in order to meet evolving social and religious needs of the Jewish community. In trying to explain biblical narratives of sex and/or violence, commentators unconsciously defend themselves against murderous, rebellious feelings against father/God. This article illustrates how commentators have defended an idealized image of the patriarch Abraham. In order to save his own life, Abraham turned his wife Sarah over to the Pharaoh who then compensated Abraham with great wealth. Commentators have censored the manifest meaning of this narrative to make it appear that God prevented Pharaoh from having sex with Sarah. Other defensive commentaries have addressed Abraham's readiness to sacrifice his son Isaac, and Jephthah's actual sacrifice of his daughter.

The Countertransference Dream

Robin Pollack-Gomolin MA

Robin Pollack-Gomolin

154 Wallis Road
Chestnut Hill, MA 02467

Robin Pollack-Gomolin   Graduate of the Master's Program of the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis, where she now is an advanced candidate in psychoanalysis and a Clinical Fellow. She is also an advanced candidate in psychoanalysis and a Clinical Fellow. She is also an advanced doctoral candidate at the Institute for the Study of Violence.

Eight clinical vignettes illustrate how the symbolic imagery of the countertransference dream assists the analyst by revealing awarenesses that are dynamic and emergent. The countertransference dream is an unconscious communication, privately recorded by the analyst. Within its discrete venue, the analyst can study the subjective and objective inductions which accompany the process of regression. Analysis of the nuanced nature of manifest representations guides the analyst's deepening awareness into a dream's unconscious essence, as well as her understanding of the transference continuum. Despite the numerous theoretical controversies associated with the production of a countertransference dream, its through analysis provides the analyst with vital clinical data. This paper posits that the countertransference dream is a measure of adjustment, as opposed to disturbance, an enactment of the most fundamental analytic intimacy: transference.

The Fear of Invasion in a Preoedipal Patient

Marc Tallent PHD

Marc Tallent

51 Fifth Avenue
New York, NY 10003

Marc Tallent   Psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City.

The concerns about invasion of a 30-year-old male in psychoanalytic treatment manifested themselves primarily through his ambivalence about entering into and sustaining intimate relationships. In the transference, his concerns with invasion expressed themselves through his use of the contact function: he was generally self-absorbed but occasionally contacted the analyst in a highly intrusive, aggressive manner. He induced two complementary countertransferential feelings: that the patient would experience contact by the analyst as invasive and harmful, or that the analyst was in danger of being invaded and harmed by the patient. The patient's concerns with invasion expressed themselves in four main ways: the desire to be passive, the desire to be penetrated, the impulse to engage in sadomasochistic interactions, and the desire to merge with the object into a boundariless state. All four manifestations were thematically related in that they served to defend against conscious awareness of aggressive impulses. Analysis of the patient's use of the contact function supported the modern psychoanalytic theory of the technique of resolving the narcissistic defense: intervening primarily in response to the patient's contacts facilitated progressive communication.

Regressive Communication in Intimate Relationships

Sara Sheftel PHD

Sara Sheftel

225 West 86th Street
New York, NY 10024

Sara Sheftel   Psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City. She is a training and supervising analyst on the faculty of the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies where she is also Director of Scientific and Cultural Affairs. She is also a member of the Editorial Board of this journal.

Regressive communication is a negative mode of engaging and maintaining contact with the other in an intimate relationship. It is repetitive and charged with negative emotions such as frustration, irritation, resentment, anger, hatred, disappointment, despair, anguish or hopelessness. Once set in motion it invariably leads to disjunction in the relationship. Its most prominent characteristic is its high degree of subjectivity, determined by unconscious processes in which regression to the developmental phase of magical thinking and infantile omnipotence plays a major role. When in that mode of relating, boundaries between self and other become blurred and give rise to distorted perceptions of reality, manifested primarily through projective identification.
